title: Problem Overview: Graph Decomposition into Cycles and Edges
content: **Erdős Problem #184** (Erdős–Gallai conjecture): Any graph on $n$ vertices can be decomposed into $O(n)$ edge-disjoint cycles and edges. Status: **OPEN**. Best known upper bound: $O(n \log^* n)$ by Bucić–Montgomery (2022). Lower bound: $(1+c)n$ from $K_{3,n-3}$.
mathContext: This is a fundamental question in **extremal graph theory**: given a graph $G = (V, E)$ with $|V| = n$, what is the minimum number of edge-disjoint cycles and single edges whose union equals $E$? The conjecture asserts this **decomposition number** $\text{dec}(G) = O(n)$. Since a tree on $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges (each requiring its own piece), the linear bound is tight up to constants. The problem sits at the intersection of cycle packing, edge partition theory, and Ramsey-type questions.

title: Mathlib Imports and Setup
content: Imports Mathlib's **SimpleGraph** and **Subgraph** modules for graph infrastructure, **Finset** for finite set operations on decomposition pieces, and **Real.log** for expressing the $O(n \log n)$ bound. Opens `Finset` namespace for cleaner notation.
mathContext: Mathlib's `SimpleGraph V` provides a foundational treatment of simple undirected graphs as symmetric irreflexive relations on vertex type $V$. The `Sym2 V` type represents unordered pairs, used to model edges. The `Fintype` and `DecidableEq` instances ensure vertices are finite and have decidable equality, enabling computable operations on the graph.

title: Cycle Structure
content: A **Cycle G** is a structure containing a list of vertices of length $\geq 3$, all distinct (`Nodup`), where consecutive vertices are adjacent in $G$ and the last vertex is adjacent to the first. This formalizes a simple cycle as an ordered vertex sequence.
mathContext: The definition requires three properties: (1) length $\geq 3$ (triangles are the shortest cycles), (2) no repeated vertices (simple cycle), and (3) adjacency along the cyclic order $v_1 v_2 \cdots v_k v_1$. The modular arithmetic `(i + 1) % length` handles the wrap-around from $v_k$ back to $v_1$. This is a **structural** definition — the cycle carries its vertex sequence, not just its edge set.

title: Single Edge as Decomposition Piece
content: A **SingleEdge G** records two vertices $u, v$ with a proof of adjacency $G.\text{Adj}\; u\; v$. These represent edges that do not belong to any cycle in the decomposition — the 'leftover' edges after cycle extraction.
mathContext: In any graph, edges on bridges (cut edges) can never be part of a cycle, so they must appear as single-edge pieces. The number of bridges provides a lower bound on the decomposition number. For a tree (all edges are bridges), $\text{dec}(T) = n - 1$, showing the linear bound is tight.

title: Decomposition Pieces and Their Edge Sets
content: **DecompPiece G** is an inductive type: either a `cycle` or an `edge`. The function **edgesOfPiece** extracts the edge set of each piece — for a cycle, the set of edges along the cyclic vertex sequence; for an edge, the singleton $\{\{u, v\}\}$.
mathContext: Edges are represented as elements of `Sym2 V` (unordered pairs), which correctly models undirected edges. The edge set of a $k$-cycle has exactly $k$ edges, while a single-edge piece contributes 1 edge. The total edge count across all pieces in a valid decomposition equals $|E(G)|$, so the decomposition number satisfies $\text{dec}(G) \leq |E(G)|$ trivially.

title: Valid Decomposition
content: **IsValidDecomposition** requires two conditions: (1) every edge of $G$ is covered by some piece, and (2) pieces are **edge-disjoint** (no edge belongs to two pieces). Together these define an **edge partition** of $G$ into cycles and edges.
mathContext: The edge-disjointness condition $\text{edgesOfPiece}(p_1) \cap \text{edgesOfPiece}(p_2) = \emptyset$ for $p_1 \neq p_2$ is what makes the problem hard. Without disjointness (mere covering), Erdős showed $n - 1$ pieces always suffice. The disjointness constraint forces careful cycle selection to avoid 'wasting' edges that could join cycles.

title: Decomposition Number
content: **decompNumber G** is axiomatized as the minimum number of pieces in any valid decomposition of $G$. The Erdős–Gallai conjecture asserts $\text{dec}(G) = O(n)$ for all graphs on $n$ vertices.
mathContext: This is axiomatized rather than defined constructively because proving the minimum exists requires showing the set of valid decomposition sizes is nonempty and bounded below — straightforward but requiring Mathlib infrastructure for `Finset.min'`. The axiomatization cleanly separates the optimization problem from the combinatorial bounds.

title: The Erdős–Gallai Conjecture
content: **ErdosGallaiConjecture**: $\exists C > 0$ such that $\text{dec}(G) \leq C \cdot n$ for all graphs $G$ on $n$ vertices. Defined as a `Prop` (not axiom), allowing it to be stated without asserting truth.
mathContext: The conjecture asks for a **universal constant** $C$ independent of the graph. The lower bound from $K_{3,n-3}$ shows $C \geq 1 + c$ for some $c > 0$, but the exact value of the optimal constant is unknown. Defining this as a `Prop` rather than an `axiom` is semantically clean: it names the conjecture without adding it to Lean's logical foundations.

title: Original Erdős–Gallai Bound: $O(n \log n)$
content: **erdos_gallai_original_bound**: There exists $C > 0$ such that $\text{dec}(G) \leq C \cdot n \cdot \log n$ for all graphs on $n \geq 2$ vertices. This was the first quantitative upper bound, proved alongside the conjecture statement.
mathContext: The $O(n \log n)$ bound was the starting point for the conjecture. The proof strategy involves iteratively extracting longest cycles: at each step, the longest cycle in the remaining graph covers many edges, and the number of iterations is bounded by $O(\log n)$ since each cycle reduces the edge count significantly. This greedy approach loses a logarithmic factor that has proven difficult to eliminate.

title: Lower Bound from $K_{3,n-3}$
content: **lower_bound_from_bipartite**: There exists $c > 0$ such that for all $n \geq 6$, some graph on $n$ vertices requires at least $(1+c)n$ pieces. The witness is the **complete bipartite graph** $K_{3,n-3}$.
mathContext: $K_{3,n-3}$ has $3(n-3)$ edges. Any cycle in a bipartite graph has even length $\geq 4$, so each cycle covers $\geq 4$ edges. With at most $3(n-3)/4$ cycles possible, additional single edges are needed, pushing the count above $n$. The precise lower bound is $(1 + c)n$ for an explicit $c > 0$ depending on the parity structure.

title: The Iterated Logarithm $\log^*$
content: **logStar n**: $\log^*(n) = 0$ if $n \leq 1$, else $1 + \log^*(\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor)$. This function grows **incredibly slowly**: $\log^*(2) = 1$, $\log^*(4) = 2$, $\log^*(16) = 3$, $\log^*(65536) = 4$, $\log^*(2^{65536}) = 5$. For any physically realizable $n$, $\log^*(n) \leq 5$.
mathContext: The iterated logarithm counts how many times one must apply $\log_2$ to reduce $n$ below 1. Its inverse is the **tower function**: $\text{tower}(k) = 2^{2^{\cdot^{\cdot^{\cdot^2}}}}$ ($k$ twos). The function appears naturally in algorithms (e.g., union-find) and combinatorics (e.g., Hales–Jewett). The $O(n \log^* n)$ bound is 'almost linear' — for all graphs up to $2^{65536}$ vertices, it is at most $5n$.

title: Bucić–Montgomery Bound: $O(n \log^* n)$ (2022)
content: **bucic_montgomery_bound**: There exists $C > 0$ such that $\text{dec}(G) \leq C \cdot n \cdot (\log^*(n) + 1)$ for all graphs on $n \geq 2$ vertices. This is the **current best** upper bound, a dramatic improvement over the original $O(n \log n)$.
mathContext: Bucić and Montgomery's proof uses a refined iterative approach: instead of extracting single longest cycles, they find **cycle decompositions of dense subgraphs** (using the Conlon–Fox–Sudakov result) and peel off layers. Each peeling step reduces the problem to a graph with lower minimum degree, and the number of layers needed is bounded by $\log^* n$. The `+1` in the bound handles the base case when $\log^*(n) = 0$.

title: Minimum Degree
content: **minDegree G** computes the minimum vertex degree in $G$ by taking the minimum over all `G.degree v`. Uses `Finset.min'` with a proof that the image set is nonempty (since `Finset.univ` is nonempty for `Fintype V`).
mathContext: Minimum degree $\delta(G) = \min_{v \in V} \deg(v)$ is a key parameter in graph theory. High minimum degree forces dense structure — when $\delta(G) \geq \varepsilon n$, the graph has $\geq \varepsilon n^2 / 2$ edges and contains long cycles. The Conlon–Fox–Sudakov result leverages this density to achieve $O(n)$ decomposition.

title: Conlon–Fox–Sudakov: Dense Case Solved (2014)
content: **conlon_fox_sudakov**: For any $\varepsilon > 0$, if $\delta(G) \geq \varepsilon n$, then $\text{dec}(G) \leq C(\varepsilon) \cdot n$. The **dense case** of the Erdős–Gallai conjecture is fully resolved — only sparse graphs remain open.
mathContext: The constant $C(\varepsilon)$ depends on $\varepsilon$ but not on $n$. The proof uses the **regularity method**: apply Szemerédi's regularity lemma to find a regular partition, then decompose edges within regular pairs into cycles using probabilistic arguments. The sparse case ($\delta(G) \ll n$) resists this approach because regularity lemma loses control at low densities.

title: Non-Disjoint Covering: $n - 1$ Pieces Suffice
content: **IsValidCovering** relaxes edge-disjointness to mere covering: every edge must appear in some piece, but pieces may overlap. **erdos_covering_bound**: in this setting, $n - 1$ cycles and edges always suffice (Erdős, 1971).
mathContext: The covering number is at most $n - 1$ because a spanning tree of $G$ uses $n - 1$ edges, and each non-tree edge creates a fundamental cycle with the tree. These $|E| - (n-1)$ cycles plus the $n - 1$ tree edges give at most $|E|$ pieces, but with clever selection one can cover all edges with $\leq n - 1$ pieces. The contrast between $n - 1$ (covering) and $\Theta(n \log^* n)$ (partition) illustrates how the disjointness constraint dramatically increases complexity.

title: Summary Theorem and $\log^*$ Verification
content: **erdos_184_summary** combines three axiomatized bounds into a conjunction: (1) $O(n \log^* n)$ upper bound, (2) $(1+c)n$ lower bound, (3) $O(n)$ for dense graphs. Proved by `exact ⟨..., ..., ...⟩`. The **key_insight_log_star** theorem verifies $\log^*(65536) = 4$ and $\log^*(4) = 2$ by `native_decide`.
mathContext: The summary theorem packages the state of knowledge: the gap between lower bound $(1+c)n$ and upper bound $O(n \log^* n)$ is a multiplicative factor of $\log^* n \leq 5$ for all practical $n$. The `native_decide` tactic evaluates the recursive `logStar` function at compile time, providing computational verification of the iterated logarithm values.
